articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Question: Where the Tourist Tax Money Actually Goes
articles.dek: Bed tax collections hit record highs last fiscal year. A Flightline review of spending records shows nearly half went to debt service on projects most visitors will never see.
brief: Escambia County collected $47.2 million in tourist development tax revenue in FY 2025, a 12% increase over the previous year
Nearly $21 million—44% of total collections—went to debt service payments on the Pensacola Bay Center and other facilities
Beach renourishment and marketing, the most visible uses of bed tax funds, received less than a quarter of total spending combined
articles.body:
The receipt arrives folded into a checkout envelope at a hotel on Pensacola Beach. A family of four from Birmingham paid $289 for two nights in a gulf-view room. Buried in the line items: $14.45 in tourist development tax. That money, multiplied across hundreds of thousands of room nights each year, feeds a $47 million annual fund that shapes what Escambia County looks like to visitors and residents alike.

Where those dollars actually land tells a different story than the one printed on Visit Pensacola brochures.

A Flightline review of Escambia County tourist development tax expenditures for fiscal year 2025 found that debt service payments consumed the largest single share of bed tax revenue—$20.8 million, or 44% of total collections. The bulk of that money services bonds on the Pensacola Bay Center, the county-owned arena that hosts concerts, hockey games and conventions roughly three miles from the beach.

Beach renourishment projects received $6.1 million. Destination marketing through Visit Pensacola got $8.4 million. Sports tourism grants and event recruitment accounted for $4.2 million. Administrative costs and reserves absorbed the remainder.

The Debt Question

The Pensacola Bay Center opened in 1985 as the Pensacola Civic Center. The county refinanced its bonds multiple times, most recently in 2019. Current debt service runs through 2038.

County records show the facility generated $2.1 million in direct revenue last fiscal year from events, parking and concessions. The gap between what the arena produces and what the county pays on its bonds gets filled by tourist tax dollars.

"The Bay Center serves tourists," said Escambia County Tourist Development Council chair Marcus Webb at a January meeting. "When you have a concert that brings 8,000 people downtown, a percentage of those are visitors staying in hotels."

How large that percentage is remains unclear. The county does not track the residency of Bay Center attendees. A 2023 economic impact study commissioned by the facility estimated 31% of ticketed event attendees came from outside Escambia and Santa Rosa counties. The methodology relied on voluntary survey responses from fewer than 400 patrons across six events.

Florida statute allows tourist development tax revenue to fund convention centers and sports facilities under certain conditions. Escambia County's local ordinance permits the same. Whether the current allocation represents the best use of visitor-generated revenue is a policy question the Tourist Development Council has not publicly revisited since 2021.

What Visitors See

The most visible bed tax expenditure—beach renourishment—received 13% of collections last year. Escambia County completed a $24 million beach restoration project in 2024, funded through a combination of tourist taxes, state grants and federal cost-sharing. The county's annual contribution covers maintenance, monitoring and reserve building for future projects.

Pensacola Beach's sand comes from offshore borrow sites and arrives by dredge. Hurricane Sally in 2020 eroded an estimated 1.2 million cubic yards of sand from county beaches. The 2024 project replaced roughly 900,000 cubic yards along a 7.5-mile stretch.

"We're in a perpetual cycle," said Santa Rosa Island Authority executive director Paolo Ghio. "The question isn't whether we'll need more sand. It's when and how much."

The next major renourishment is tentatively scheduled for 2029. Cost projections range from $28 million to $35 million depending on sand availability and fuel prices.

Marketing Pensacola

Visit Pensacola, the county's destination marketing organization, operates as a division of the county government rather than an independent nonprofit—a structure that differs from peer destinations like Visit Panama City Beach and Visit Mobile.

The organization's $8.4 million budget funded television and digital advertising campaigns, travel writer familiarization trips, trade show attendance and a staff of 14. The largest single expenditure was a $2.3 million contract with a Birmingham-based advertising agency for media placement.

Measuring marketing effectiveness is notoriously difficult. Visit Pensacola tracks website traffic, social media engagement and a metric called "influenced visitation" that attempts to correlate advertising exposure with actual hotel bookings. The organization reported 127,000 influenced room nights in FY 2025, a figure that relies on modeling assumptions the county has not independently verified.

"We're competing with destinations that spend three and four times what we do," said Visit Pensacola director Darien Schaefer. "Destin, Panama City Beach, Gulf Shores—they all have larger marketing budgets and longer beach seasons."

Schaefer requested a 15% budget increase for FY 2026. The Tourist Development Council recommended 8%. The Board of County Commissioners has not yet voted on the allocation.

The Sports Gamble

Escambia County has aggressively pursued sports tourism over the past decade, recruiting baseball tournaments, soccer showcases and running events to fill hotel rooms during shoulder seasons.

The strategy requires upfront investment. The county spent $1.8 million last year on grants to event organizers—payments that cover facility rentals, marketing support and sometimes direct subsidies to guarantee minimum participation.

The return on that investment is measured in hotel room nights. County staff estimate sports events generated 47,000 room nights in FY 2025, producing roughly $2.4 million in tourist tax revenue. The math appears favorable: $1.8 million in spending yielding $2.4 million in direct tax return, plus secondary economic activity.

But the calculation depends on assumptions about what economists call "but-for" spending—money that would not have been spent in Escambia County absent the recruited event. If a youth baseball tournament simply shifts families from one destination to another, the regional economic impact is smaller than raw attendance figures suggest.

"We don't have perfect data," acknowledged county tourism development director Amy Nicholson. "We know how many room nights get booked. We don't always know what those families would have done otherwise."

The Accountability Gap

The Tourist Development Council meets monthly in a county administrative building three blocks from Pensacola Bay. Meetings typically last 90 minutes. Attendance by the public is sparse—often single digits.

The council includes hotel operators, tourism industry representatives and two county commissioners. Members serve staggered terms. Vacancies sometimes go unfilled for months.

Agendas and minutes are posted online, usually within two weeks of meetings. Detailed expenditure reports are available through public records requests but are not proactively published. The Flightline obtained spending breakdowns through three separate requests over a six-week period.

Comparable Florida counties handle transparency differently. Walton County publishes quarterly tourist tax reports on its website with line-item detail. Bay County streams TDC meetings live and archives video recordings.

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, who sits on the TDC, said he would support more detailed public reporting.

"People pay these taxes and they have a right to know where the money goes," Bergosh said. "Whether we're getting the best return on that investment is a fair question."

The Board of County Commissioners is scheduled to review FY 2026 tourist development tax allocations at its July 15 meeting. The proposed budget maintains current spending ratios, with debt service consuming the largest share through at least 2030.

That family from Birmingham has already gone home. Their $14.45 contribution joined millions of others in a fund that keeps an arena's lights on, puts sand on a beach, and buys television ads that might convince someone else to make the same trip. Whether the balance is right depends on who's asking—and whether anyone's listening to the answer.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The Crane Count: Downtown Pensacola Has 6 Active Construction Sites. Here's What's Rising.
articles.dek: From the Southtowne apartments to the Jefferson Street hotel project, a ground-level tour of what's being built, what's stalled, and what the skyline will look like by 2028.
brief: Six major construction projects are actively underway in downtown Pensacola, with combined investment exceeding $180 million
The 12-story Southtowne apartment tower on Main Street represents the tallest new residential building downtown in three decades
Two projects that broke ground in 2024 remain stalled due to financing issues, leaving fenced lots on Palafox and Intendencia streets
articles.body:
Stand at the corner of Main and Palafox on a Tuesday morning and count the cranes. There are three visible from this spot alone. A fourth rises behind the old Escambia County courthouse. Two more work the waterfront.

Six active construction sites. More than $180 million in combined investment. And a downtown skyline that will look noticeably different by the time these projects finish in 2027 and 2028.

The Flightline spent two weeks walking every block of the urban core, photographing progress, pulling permits, and talking to project managers about timelines. Here's what's rising, what's stalled, and what Pensacola will look like when the cranes come down.

Southtowne Apartments: The Tallest New Thing Downtown

The tower crane at 101 South Main Street stands 160 feet tall. It needs to be. The building beneath it will reach 12 stories when complete—the tallest new residential structure downtown since the 1990s.

Southtowne, developed by Mobile-based Harbert Realty Services, broke ground in October 2025. Workers have completed the parking podium and poured concrete for the first four floors of the residential tower above it.

"We're tracking about two weeks ahead of schedule," said project superintendent Marcus Webb during a hardhat tour last Thursday. "The concrete crews have been getting good weather windows."

The finished building will hold 186 apartments—a mix of studios, one-bedrooms and two-bedrooms ranging from $1,650 to $2,400 per month according to pre-leasing materials. Ground-floor retail space totaling 8,200 square feet remains uncommitted.

Target completion: March 2028.

The Jefferson Street Hotel

Three blocks north, a different kind of project rises on the site of the old Pensacola News Journal parking lot at Jefferson and Baylen streets.

This one is a 156-room boutique hotel flagged under Marriott's Tribute Portfolio brand. The developer, Innisfree Hotels of Gulf Breeze, secured $42 million in construction financing last spring after two years of negotiations with the city over parking arrangements and stormwater infrastructure.

The building topped out in April. Workers are now installing the curtain wall facade—a mix of glass and terracotta panels meant to echo the brick warehouses that once lined this stretch of Jefferson.

"We wanted something that felt like it belonged here," said Innisfree CEO Patricia Grant. "Not another glass box that could be anywhere."

The hotel will include a rooftop bar with views of Pensacola Bay and a ground-floor restaurant operated by a local hospitality group Grant declined to name. The company expects to begin hiring staff in early 2027 for a spring opening.

Two Waterfront Projects Racing to Finish

The Community Maritime Park district, west of downtown proper, hosts two simultaneous construction sites separated by a single fence.

The larger of the two is a 94-unit condominium building called The Moorings at 351 West Main Street. Prices for the two- and three-bedroom units range from $485,000 to $1.2 million. About 60 percent of units have sold according to developer Coastal Residential Partners.

The structure reached its full eight stories in February. Interior fit-out is underway. From the street, the building looks nearly complete—gleaming white balconies facing the bay, landscaping crews working the perimeter.

"We're doing final inspections floor by floor," said site manager Renee Dawson. "First closings should happen in September."

Next door, a smaller mixed-use building called Harborview is rising at 375 West Main. This four-story structure will hold 32 apartments above 4,000 square feet of commercial space. It's the second phase of a project whose first phase—a 48-unit building—opened in 2023.

Both waterfront projects benefit from Community Redevelopment Area funds that helped finance public improvements including wider sidewalks and a new segment of the bay walk.

The Palafox Renovation That Became Something Else

At 433 South Palafox Street, a century-old brick building is being gutted to its bones.

The original plan called for a straightforward renovation—new mechanical systems, code upgrades, cosmetic work. Then contractors opened the walls.

"The structural situation was worse than anyone expected," said architect David Chen of Pensacola-based Chen Architecture + Design. "We essentially had to rebuild the entire rear section of the building."

What started as a $3 million renovation became a $7 million reconstruction. The project lost 14 months to redesign and re-permitting.

The finished building will house a law firm on the upper floors and retail on the ground level. Chen said the facade will be restored to its 1920s appearance using historical photographs as a guide.

"It cost more and took longer, but the building will last another hundred years," Chen said. "You can't say that about a lot of new construction."

What's Stalled

Not everything that broke ground has kept moving.

A fenced lot at 200 East Intendencia Street has sat unchanged for 18 months. The site was supposed to hold a 72-unit apartment building. Permits were issued in March 2024. Foundation work began that summer.

Then construction stopped.

The developer, a Jacksonville-based LLC called Coastal Urban Partners, has not responded to multiple interview requests. City records show no new permits have been pulled. No work has occurred since August 2024.

Escambia County property records show a notice of lis pendens—an indicator of pending litigation—was filed against the property in January 2026 by a Miami-based lender. The notice suggests a dispute over the construction loan.

A similar situation exists at 15 South Palafox Street, where a mixed-use project was announced with fanfare in 2023. The developer erected a fence and demolished a small structure on the site in early 2024. Nothing has happened since.

That developer, Atlanta-based Perimeter Development Group, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September 2025. The Pensacola property is listed among the company's assets in bankruptcy filings. Its fate will be decided by a federal judge in Atlanta.

What Comes Next

The six active projects represent only part of what's in the pipeline.

The Pensacola City Council has approved site plans for three additional downtown projects that have not yet broken ground: a 200-unit apartment building on Garden Street, a boutique hotel on Romana Street, and a mixed-use development on the former Pensacola Parking Authority lot on Chase Street.

All three have valid permits. All three developers have told city officials they intend to begin construction within the next 12 months.

Whether they actually do depends on financing markets, construction costs and a dozen other variables outside anyone's control.

For now, the cranes keep turning. The concrete keeps pouring. And downtown Pensacola keeps changing, one floor at a time.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Begins Friday. Road Closures, Crowds, and What the Base Wants You to Know.
articles.dek: NAS Pensacola expects 150,000 visitors for the annual air show. New security protocols mean longer lines at the gate this year.
brief: Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show runs Friday through Sunday at NAS Pensacola, with gates opening at 8 a.m. each day
New DoD security protocols require all adults to present government-issued ID; base officials recommend arriving before 9 a.m. to avoid hour-plus waits
Radford Boulevard, Blue Angel Parkway, and portions of Navy Boulevard will see rolling closures during practice and show times
articles.body:
The F/A-18 Super Hornets were already screaming over Pensacola Bay by 11 a.m. Tuesday. Practice runs for the Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show have turned the sky into a stage all week, a preview of what 150,000 visitors will see when gates open Friday morning at Naval Air Station Pensacola.

This year's show marks the 78th homecoming for the Navy's flight demonstration squadron, and base officials say it will also be the most security-intensive in recent memory.

"We want everyone to come out and enjoy the show," said Capt. Marcus Webb, commanding officer of NAS Pensacola, at a media briefing Monday. "But we need folks to understand this is an active military installation. New Department of Defense protocols are in place, and that means longer processing times at every gate."

What's Different This Year

The changes stem from a DoD-wide security directive issued in March following incidents at other installations. Every adult entering the base must now present a government-issued photo ID. Children under 16 are exempt but must be accompanied by an adult with valid identification.

Previously, vehicle checks at the main gates were the primary screening method. Now, base security will conduct individual ID verification for all passengers before vehicles proceed to parking areas.

Webb estimated wait times could exceed 90 minutes during peak arrival hours between 10 a.m. and noon. He urged visitors to arrive before 9 a.m. or after 1 p.m. to avoid the worst congestion.

"If you're pulling up at 10:30, you're going to be sitting in your car for a while," Webb said. "Plan accordingly."

Road Closures and Traffic Plans

The Escambia County Sheriff's Office and Pensacola Police Department will manage traffic flow on roads leading to the base. Expect rolling closures and heavy congestion on:

  • Navy Boulevard from Fairfield Drive to the main gate
  • Blue Angel Parkway from Gulf Beach Highway to the west gate
  • Radford Boulevard between Barrancas Avenue and the back gate

Deputies will close lanes as needed to keep traffic moving toward base entrances. Southbound Blue Angel Parkway will be restricted to air show traffic only from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. Friday through Sunday.

"We've done this before. We know the chokepoints," said Lt. David Farrell with ECSO's traffic division. "But 150,000 people is 150,000 people. There's only so much asphalt."

Residents of Warrington and the areas surrounding NAS Pensacola should expect delays for routine trips throughout the weekend. Farrell recommended using I-10 and alternative routes when possible.

Schedule and Performers

Gates open at 8 a.m. each day. The air show begins at 10 a.m. with civilian aerobatic performers and military demonstration teams. The Blue Angels take the sky at 2 p.m. for their full demonstration, weather permitting.

This year's lineup includes the U.S. Army Golden Knights parachute team, the GEICO Skytypers, and solo performances from several civilian aerobatic pilots. Static displays of military aircraft will be open for viewing near the flight line.

Friday is traditionally the lightest attendance day. Saturday draws the largest crowds. Sunday offers a slightly shorter show schedule, with the Blue Angels flying at 1:30 p.m.

What to Bring, What to Leave

Coolers are permitted but will be searched. No glass containers, alcohol, drones, or weapons of any kind. Folding chairs and blankets are encouraged. Strollers are allowed but may slow security processing.

Food and beverage vendors will be stationed throughout the viewing areas. ATMs will be available, but base officials recommend bringing cash to speed transactions.

Pets are not permitted except for documented service animals.

The base is also asking visitors to leave professional camera equipment with lenses longer than six inches at home unless they have obtained prior media credentials through the NAS Pensacola public affairs office.

Weather Concerns

The National Weather Service forecast for Pensacola shows a 40 percent chance of afternoon thunderstorms Saturday and Sunday. If lightning is detected within 10 miles of the base, all flight operations halt and spectators are directed to seek shelter in vehicles or designated buildings.

"We don't fly through storms, and we don't put spectators at risk," Webb said. "If we have to delay or cancel portions of the show, we will."

There are no rain dates scheduled. Decisions on weather delays are made day-of based on conditions.

The Homecoming Tradition

The Blue Angels were established in 1946 and have called Pensacola home since their founding. The homecoming show is both a community celebration and a family reunion of sorts for the squadron, whose members spend most of the year traveling to air shows across the country.

"This is where we live. This is where our families are," said Cmdr. Alex Turner, the Blue Angels' flight leader and commanding officer. "Flying over Pensacola Bay in front of the people who support us year-round—there's nothing like it."

For Turner, this will be his second and final homecoming as flight leader. He is scheduled to rotate out of the squadron in November.

"I'm going to enjoy every second of it," he said.
